[[File:Pappa col Pomodoro.ogv|thumb|A common method of cooking the dish]]
{{lang|it|'''Pappa al pomodoro'''}} ({{IPA|it|ˈpappa al pomoˈdɔːro|lang}}; translating to 'tomato<ref>{{cite book|last=Frascarelli|first=Mara|title=The Syntax-Phonology Interface in Focus and Topic Constructions in Italian|year=2000|publisher=Kluwer|location=Dordrecht [u.a.]|isbn=978-0-7923-6240-1|page=26|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R6bP25yLQAAC&q=%22Pasta+al+pomodoro%22&pg=PA26}}</ref> mush') is a thick Tuscan [[bread soup]] typically prepared with fresh [[tomato]]es, [[bread]], [[olive oil]], [[garlic]], [[basil]], and various other fresh ingredients.<ref name="History" /> The bread is usually [[stale]] or leftover.<ref name="History" /> A basic preparation of ''{{lang|it|pappa al pomodoro}}'' involves lightly frying the garlic in oil, before briefly cooking it in a soup with the tomatoes, bread, and basil.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Riley |first=Gillian |author-link=Gillian Riley |url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont0000rile_q4o3/ |title=The Oxford Companion to Italian Food |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-19-860617-8 |location=New York |pages=360–361 |url-access=limited}}</ref> The dish is sometimes served hot, and at other times at room temperature or chilled. A rule upheld as a Tuscan tradition in Italy is that cheese must not be added within or on top of the dish.<ref name="History" /> 

''{{lang|it|Pappa al pomodoro}}'' originated with the Tuscan [[tenant farmer]] as a way to use their meagre supply of tomatoes. Stale bread was used because it was the only type available in rural areas, where communal ovens were lit once per week to bake the week's bread supply.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Gentilcore |first=David |author-link=David Gentilcore |url=https://archive.org/details/historyoftomatoi0000davi/ |title=Pomodoro! A History of the Tomato in Italy |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-231-15206-8 |location=New York |pages=96 |url-access=limited}}</ref> 

The dish became known in Italy outside of Tuscany with the publication of the serial ''[[Il Giornalino di Gian Burrasca]]'' from 1907–1908. "Long live ''{{lang|it|pappa al pomodoro}}''" served as the catchphrase of the story's hero, a child named "Johnny Hurricane" in protest of the bland soups served at the boarding school he was forced to attend.<ref name=":0" /> Further awareness came with the story's television adaptation in the 1960s, in which [[Rita Pavone]] sang the well-known song "[[Viva la pappa col pomodoro]]".<ref name="History">{{cite web|last=Tibaldi|first=Andrea|title=Pappa al pomodoro|language=it|url=http://www.cibo360.it/cucina/mondo/pappa_al_pomodoro.htm|website=CIBO360.it|publisher=Wellness Gourmet|accessdate=November 11, 2014}}</ref>
